The thermal analysis data also provides some evidence in favor of the higher peritectic temperature (1302 K±2 K) while thermal analysis combined with microscopy indicates a peritectic liquid composition of 13.5 wt.%±0.5 wt.% (27.91 at%±0.86at.%), which is in close agreement with Okamoto’s proposed value of 13.43 wt.% (27.8 at.%). It should be noted here that H. Okamoto (2012) relied heavily on the construction by Berche et al. (2011) for the solidus and liquidus. That said, due to the more steeply rising initial slope, the Mardon et al. (1959) definitions are closer to the current data set in the low-Mo region. These two models are each supported, but differ in some fine detail. Further refinement of the thermodynamic models will likely hinge upon recalculation after further examination of the peritectic reaction. Repeated TA measurements under three different heating/cooling rates provide the main set of data for the liquidus and solidus boundaries as well as the associated uncertainty in this study. Solidification and melting signals are also both used because they give different and complementary information. Sampling during heating/melting theoretically provides the best measure of the liquidus; however, instrument lag can make the signal difficult to determine accurately. Inversely, initiation of solidification is theoretically unsuitable when taken in isolation because nucleation requires finite, and sometimes significant, levels of undercooling and the inherent stochasticiy introduces additional variation. Plotting both sets of information together can, however, provide important bounds of behavior. In Figure 4, the nucleation temperature symbols point up to denote that the liquidus must be above the measurement. The endset temperatures point down to indicate that the real liquidus must be below this temperature. The nature of these bounds in relation to the true equilibrium liquidus requires some explanation.
